analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations and investment funds from buying new U.S. farmland.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and has seen no further action, with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for corporations, pension funds, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and other large investment vehicles to buy or hold U.S. farmland. Only entities owned by 25 or fewer people who actually work the land could acquire farmland going forward, with carve-outs for research, nonprofits, municipalities, farmer co-ops, and land seized for unpaid debts. Existing corporate owners could keep what they have but would lose access to USDA programs and Farm Credit System loans. Violators could face forced divestiture, civil penalties up to twice the land's value, and up to 5 years in prison for knowingly breaking the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers, new and beginning farmers, and rural communities. The bill's findings state that farmland prices have nearly doubled since 2005 and that deep-pocketed corporate buyers can often outbid independent farmers; by taking funds and corporations out of the bidding, the bill aims to keep land in reach of people who work it. Farmer- and rancher-owned cooperatives and heirs'-property owners are explicitly allowed to hold land. Retiring farmers lose nothing in selling to individuals or small farm partnerships.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers and aspiring farm buyers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any 'unauthorized legal entity' — including corporations, pension funds, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and multilayered holding structures — from acquiring or holding an ownership interest in agricultural land, directly or indirectly, with perjury-signed affidavits filed at purchase and with each federal tax return to verify compliance.

Caps legal ownership structures at entities with no more than 25 owners, all of whom must be natural persons 'actively engaged in farming' — with 'solely providing capital' expressly excluded — so land ownership stays with people who work the land rather than passive investors.

Backs the ban with real teeth: the Attorney General can sue to force divestiture within one year (with court-ordered public sale if they don't), the Agriculture Secretary can levy civil penalties of up to 2 times the land's fair market value per violation, knowing violations carry up to 5 years' imprisonment, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents for additional penalties of up to $1 million or the land's value.
Cuts existing unauthorized corporate owners out of USDA programs and Farm Credit System lending, and directs the Secretary to report violations publicly to Congress each year.
Authorizes states to impose rules at least as strict as the federal ban, preserving tougher state-level farmland ownership laws.

analysis.who_pays: Institutional and corporate buyers of farmland: pension funds, mutual funds, life-insurance separate accounts, REITs, and investment companies, which could no longer add farmland to their portfolios; existing corporate farmland owners, who could keep current holdings but could not expand and would lose USDA program and Farm Credit System eligibility; and corporations seeking land for future farming, who would face civil penalties up to 2x land value, divestiture orders, and criminal exposure for knowing violations. Retiring farmers selling large parcels could also see a smaller buyer pool.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pension funds, REITs, and farmland investors

drawbacks.text: The bill shrinks the pool of legitimate farmland buyers to individuals and small farming partnerships, which would likely reduce prices at the top of the market. The bill's own findings call farmland 'a source of wealth, including generational wealth' — for retiring farmers whose land is their retirement nest egg, a smaller buyer pool could mean selling for less.

Family succession could get harder: ownership is limited to entities whose owners are all 'actively engaged in farming,' and merely providing capital does not count. Land held in an irrevocable trust for heirs who don't farm doesn't clearly fit the bill's exceptions (which cover fiduciaries and revocable trusts but not all family trusts), so some ordinary estate-planning arrangements could become noncompliant.

The 25-owner, all-active-farmer cap would prevent mid-sized farm businesses from raising outside capital even from individual investors, potentially limiting growth for farms larger than a single family can finance.

The bill classifies pension funds as unauthorized buyers, so retirement funds could no longer add farmland — an asset class some funds hold to diversify retiree portfolios — which fund managers would argue comes at their beneficiaries' expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and documented trend — the bill's findings state that institutionally owned farm properties tripled from 2005 to 2025, growing from under $2 billion to over $16 billion in value, while farmland prices nearly doubled — and the exemption list is thoughtfully drawn, covering co-ops, heirs' property, nonprofits, research land, and debt-driven foreclosures. But it is a blunt instrument: the definitions sweep in pension funds, some family trusts, and farm businesses with non-farming co-owners, and compliance would depend on affidavits rather than robust verification. The core tradeoff — cheaper land for working farmers versus reduced sale values and less investment capital for landowners — is a genuine one that an honest supporter should acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on April 27, 2026, on behalf of himself and Sen. Bernie Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or additional cosponsors — appears in the action history, and the 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet, since the bill has not advanced; institutional farmland investors benefit for now because no federal restriction on new corporate farmland purchases has moved.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Farmland for Farmers Act of 2026 on April 27, 2026.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, making it a two-sponsor measure.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Democrat and one Independent have sponsored the bill, and no committee or floor vote has yet revealed any partisan split.

industries.industry: Institutional farmland investors (pension funds, investment funds, REITs)
industries.note: The bill bars these funds from acquiring or holding any new agricultural land, cutting them out of a market where the bill says their holdings grew from under $2 billion to over $16 billion between 2005 and 2025. Their gain in that market comes from bidding land away from family farmers, so their interest runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

They can keep land owned on enactment, but cannot expand, must file compliance affidavits, and lose eligibility for every USDA program and Farm Credit System loan. Grandfathering softens the hit but the bill treats their ownership as the problem it aims to stop growing.
The bill explicitly authorizes farmer- and rancher-controlled cooperatives with one vote per member, placing them alongside family farmers as the preferred owners of agricultural land.

The bill makes compliance documentation a condition of Farm Credit System participation and disqualifies unauthorized entities holding grandfathered land, adding underwriting duties but aligning the system's lending with owner-operators.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no hearing, and no action beyond referral to the Senate Agriculture Committee, the bill will most likely sit until the Congress ends in January 2027. A farmland-ownership restriction of this scope would realistically need to attach to the next farm bill or a similar vehicle to move; as a standalone bill with this level of support, its odds are low. Roughly a dozen states already restrict corporate farm ownership, so the policy idea continues to advance mainly at the state level.
